questions.knowledge_point: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the First Result
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+(kx)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(kx)+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\sqrt{3}/6}\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{\sqrt{3}/6}\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{\sqrt{3}/6}\frac{1}{1+(2t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2t)]}_{a}^{\sqrt{3}/6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{\pi }{6}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x)]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x)]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14052212/assets/4612e37c6c611cbaa44c09f4dcc47d006ad45403fff9af5b4df7dca71693dd6e.png)

 

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\sqrt{3}/6}\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{\pi }{6}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⟹\,2\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(u)]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)] \\  & =2\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]-\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14052212/assets/46e6cf2950c99831a7445a862fb36a6a7b8f9233a82e49c7cf5da4a383ec4756.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & =2\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u={t}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=3{t}^{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{t}^{2}\text{d}t.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $t\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={t}^{3}$ is as follows:

| $t$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3{t}^{2}}{1+25{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{1}{1+25{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3{t}^{2}}{1+25{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{1}{1+25{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{1+25{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(5u)]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5u)]_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5a)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5a)]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5x),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5x)]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5x)]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14052212/assets/06f99111a041ff564ece3019e7dba5331bb4f225d224dff07bb92d83f4e33eb2.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3{t}^{2}}{1+25{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5a)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the Second Result
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \frac{1}{{k}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{k})+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}x & =12\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =12\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{3}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =12\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})]}_{a}^{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =4\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{3})) \\  & =4\cdot (\frac{\pi }{6}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{3})).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3}),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14052212/assets/24ca4823d220c3eb31127ed28ab7c75b1297e10ae20a1926d112a234806c411e.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}x & =4\cdot (\frac{\pi }{6}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{3})) \\  & =4\cdot (\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =4\cdot (\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{5}\frac{6}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{5}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{5}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{5}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{5})]}_{a}^{5} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{5})) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{4}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{5})).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{5}),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{5})=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{5})=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14052212/assets/f8325b1ea152bd40aaa909202bfce59e621952486041c657c0e27b9192ecec03.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{5}\frac{6}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{4}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{5})) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{4}-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot \frac{3\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$
